datenschutz-grundprinzipien-01.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the principles listed in Art. 5(1) GDPR for processing personal data?

options.a: Data minimisation: only data that is actually necessary for the purpose may be collected
options.b: Storage limitation: data may not be kept longer than necessary
options.c: Profit maximisation: processing must serve the company's economic success
options.d: Accuracy: data must be factually correct and kept up to date where necessary

datenschutz-grundprinzipien-01.explanation: Art. 5(1) GDPR lists seven principles: lawfulness/fairness/transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity and confidentiality, plus accountability (Art. 5(2)). Economic benefit to the company is not a data protection principle in its own right - at most it can feed into a legitimate interest under Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR, but it never replaces the other duties.

datenschutz-grundprinzipien-02.question: HR has stored an employee's private email address solely to process payroll. May the marketing department simply use that address to send her advertising for internal employee perks?

options.a: Yes, once data is lawfully held anywhere in the company it may be reused for any internal purpose
options.b: No, that would violate purpose limitation - reusing data for a different purpose needs its own legal basis or a compatibility check
options.c: Yes, because this is internal communication within the same employer and GDPR only governs data shared externally
options.d: No, but only because it is a private rather than a work email address

datenschutz-grundprinzipien-02.explanation: The purpose-limitation principle (Art. 5(1)(b) GDPR) means personal data collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes may not simply be reused for an incompatible purpose. Reuse is only permitted after a compatibility assessment (Art. 6(4) GDPR) or on the strength of a new, separate legal basis - 'the company already has it' is not sufficient justification.

datenschutz-grundprinzipien-03.question: Which of the following is NOT an independent legal basis under Art. 6(1) GDPR for processing personal data?

options.a: Processing is necessary for the performance of a contract with the data subject
options.b: The data subject has validly given consent to the processing
options.c: Processing is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation to which the controller is subject
options.d: Processing merely makes internal workflows more convenient and saves cost

datenschutz-grundprinzipien-03.explanation: Art. 6(1) GDPR recognises six legal bases: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, and legitimate interest. Mere operational convenience or cost savings is not, by itself, any of these six - at most it can feed into the balancing-of-interests test under Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR, where it still has to be weighed against the data subject's interests.

datenschutz-grundprinzipien-04.question: What does the accountability principle under Art. 5(2) GDPR actually require of the controller?

options.a: They must not only comply with the data protection principles but also be able to demonstrate that compliance, e.g. through documentation, records, and policies
options.b: They must obtain prior approval from the supervisory authority for every processing activity
options.c: They must issue an annual public press release accounting for all data breaches
options.d: They must publish all processing activities for free public inspection by anyone

datenschutz-grundprinzipien-04.explanation: Accountability means it is not enough to actually comply with data protection law - the controller must also be able to prove that compliance at any time, for example through a record of processing activities (Art. 30 GDPR), internal policies, training records, or data protection impact assessments. There is no general requirement to get prior authority approval for each processing activity, and no duty to issue a public press release for every activity.

datenschutz-grundprinzipien-05.question: A company wants to process customer data for fraud prevention without obtaining consent, relying on a legitimate interest under Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR. What is strictly required for this?

options.a: There must be an actually existing legitimate interest, the processing must be necessary to achieve it, and a balancing test must not show that the data subjects' interests or fundamental rights override it
options.b: It is enough that management considers the processing sensible - a balancing test against customers' interests is not legally required
options.c: A legitimate interest may only be invoked by public authorities, never by private companies
options.d: Legitimate interest is only permissible if the data is subsequently sold on to credit reporting agencies

datenschutz-grundprinzipien-05.explanation: Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR requires a three-part test: (1) an actually existing legitimate interest of the controller or a third party, (2) necessity of the processing to achieve that interest, and (3) a balancing test in which the data subject's interests, fundamental rights and freedoms must not override it. Merely deeming the processing 'sensible' from a business standpoint, without a genuine balancing test, is not sufficient, and this basis is available to both public and private bodies.

datenschutz-grundprinzipien-06.question: A customer withdraws by phone a consent to data processing that was originally given with a single click on the company's website. The company then insists the withdrawal must additionally be submitted in writing by post within 14 days, claiming that only this is a 'proper' way to process it. Is that permissible?

options.a: Yes, because withdrawal must generally take the same form as a written contract
options.b: No, under Art. 7(3) GDPR withdrawing consent must be as easy as giving it - imposing a more burdensome procedure solely for withdrawal is not permitted
options.c: Yes, as long as the company has specified this in its terms and conditions
options.d: No, because withdrawing consent always retroactively makes all prior processing unlawful

datenschutz-grundprinzipien-06.explanation: Art. 7(3) GDPR expressly states that withdrawing consent must be as easy as giving it. If consent was given with a single click, withdrawal may not be made subject to stricter formal requirements (e.g. a written letter by post). Withdrawal also only has effect for the future - it does not affect the lawfulness of processing carried out before the withdrawal.

datenschutz-grundprinzipien-07.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the conditions listed in Art. 4(11) GDPR for a valid consent?

options.a: It must be given voluntarily for the specific case
options.b: It must be given in an informed manner, i.e. the data subject must know what they are consenting to
options.c: It must be given unambiguously, e.g. through a clear affirmative action
options.d: It must always be given on paper with a handwritten signature - an electronic or other clear affirmative action is not sufficient

datenschutz-grundprinzipien-07.explanation: Art. 4(11) GDPR defines consent as any freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication of the data subject's wishes, given by a statement or by a clear affirmative action. No particular form such as a handwritten signature on paper is required - a click, a checkbox, or another clear affirmative action is sufficient as long as it meets these characteristics.

datenschutz-grundprinzipien-08.question: A company introduces a time-tracking system that also creates movement profiles of employees, and regulates details in a works agreement with the works council. Which statement about Art. 88 GDPR is correct?

options.a: Art. 88 GDPR completely prohibits works agreements on employee data protection, since only state legislation is permitted
options.b: Art. 88 GDPR allows member states to establish more specific rules for processing employee data through legislation or collective agreements such as works agreements, which must however include appropriate measures to safeguard human dignity and fundamental rights
options.c: A works agreement can fall short of GDPR requirements to any extent, as long as employer and works council agree
options.d: Art. 88 GDPR only applies to recruitment processes, not to existing employment relationships

datenschutz-grundprinzipien-08.explanation: Art. 88 GDPR gives member states the option to establish, through legislation or collective agreements - in Germany, for example, works agreements or collective bargaining agreements - more specific rules to protect employees' rights and freedoms when processing their personal data in the employment context. Under Art. 88(2) GDPR, such rules must include suitable and specific measures to safeguard employees' human dignity, legitimate interests and fundamental rights - so they may only make GDPR protections more concrete, not fall below them.

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-01.question: An employee submits a request to HR for access to the data held about them (Art. 15 GDPR). Within what timeframe must the company generally respond?

options.a: Within 72 hours, as with a data breach
options.b: Without undue delay and at the latest within one month of receiving the request; a further two-month extension is possible for complex cases, with reasons given
options.c: There is no statutory deadline - a response 'within a reasonable time' is always sufficient
options.d: Within one year, since access requests rank behind day-to-day business

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-01.explanation: Under Art. 12(3) GDPR, the controller must provide information on the action taken without undue delay and in any event within one month of receiving the request. For multiple or complex requests, this can be extended by a further two months, but the data subject must be informed of the extension within the first month. Missing the deadline is a serious compliance failure that can trigger a complaint to the supervisory authority.

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-02.question: A former employee, six months after leaving, demands complete deletion of her payslips (Art. 17 GDPR). How should the company respond?

options.a: Delete immediately, since every erasure request must be executed within 72 hours without exception
options.b: Refuse, because the right to erasure generally does not apply to former employees
options.c: Not fully grant the request to the extent statutory retention obligations (e.g. tax and commercial-law retention periods) prevent deletion - that data must be retained for now but restricted from other use
options.d: Delete it, but only if the former employee first provides written confirmation from the tax authority

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-02.explanation: The right to erasure under Art. 17 GDPR generally does apply to former employees too, but it is limited by Art. 17(3)(b) GDPR where processing is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation (e.g. commercial/tax retention periods under German commercial and tax law). In such cases the data must be kept until the retention period expires but may no longer be used for other purposes. A blanket refusal or an unchecked 72-hour deletion would both be wrong.

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-03.question: What does the 'right to data portability' under Art. 20 GDPR actually mean?

options.a: The right to have a company forward personal data to any third party without limit
options.b: The right to receive data provided to a controller - where processing is based on consent or contract and carried out by automated means - in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format, or to have it transmitted directly to another controller
options.c: The right to a free physical paper copy of all files, regardless of the legal basis for processing
options.d: The right to have data automatically transferred to a new employer after one year

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-03.explanation: Art. 20 GDPR only covers data the data subject provided themselves, where processing is based on consent or a contract and is carried out by automated means. Its purpose is to make it easier to switch between providers or services, not to create a general obligation to pass data to third parties or a right to paper copies regardless of the legal basis.

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-04.question: A customer objects to their data being processed for direct marketing purposes. How must the company respond?

options.a: Processing for marketing purposes must stop immediately and without exception - for direct marketing, the company has no 'balancing of interests' option
options.b: The company may continue the marketing if it can demonstrate an overriding legitimate interest
options.c: The company only has to honour the objection if the customer provides a justification
options.d: There is no legal right to object to marketing, only a right to withdraw a consent that was previously given

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-04.explanation: For direct marketing, the right to object under Art. 21(2) and (3) GDPR is an absolute right: as soon as the data subject objects, their data may no longer be processed for that purpose - unlike the general objection right in Art. 21(1) GDPR, there is no balancing-of-interests test here, and no justification is required from the customer.

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-05.question: An employee notices that their date of birth was recorded incorrectly in their personnel file. Which right can they invoke for this?

options.a: The right to rectification under Art. 16 GDPR - the controller must correct inaccurate personal data without undue delay and may also have to complete incomplete data
options.b: Only the right to erasure under Art. 17 GDPR, since inaccurate data must always be deleted entirely
options.c: The right to data portability under Art. 20 GDPR, since they can bring the correct data themselves
options.d: None at all, since corrections in an employment relationship are only possible through a court claim

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-05.explanation: Art. 16 GDPR grants the data subject the right to obtain from the controller, without undue delay, rectification of inaccurate personal data concerning them; taking into account the purposes of the processing, they can also request completion of incomplete data, for instance by providing a supplementary statement. Erasure is not the right tool here, since the data is still needed - just needs to be correct - and going to court is not a mandatory prerequisite.

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-06.question: A customer disputes the accuracy of her address stored by the company and asks that the data not be used further while this is being clarified, but also not be deleted. Which right describes this situation?

options.a: The right to erasure under Art. 17 GDPR, since disputed data must always be removed immediately
options.b: The right to data portability under Art. 20 GDPR
options.c: The right to restriction of processing under Art. 18(1)(a) GDPR - while the accuracy is being verified, the data may generally only be stored, not otherwise processed
options.d: There is no distinct right for this - the customer must either request erasure or nothing at all

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-06.explanation: Art. 18(1) GDPR gives the data subject the right to obtain restriction of processing, among other cases where they contest the accuracy of the data (lit. a), for a period allowing the controller to verify it. Restricted data may then, apart from storage, generally only be processed with consent, to establish or defend legal claims, to protect another person's rights, or for important public interest reasons. This is a distinct intermediate tool between doing nothing and full erasure.

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-07.question: A new customer provides their data directly to the company when concluding a contract. What obligation does the company have at that moment under Art. 13 GDPR?

options.a: No special obligation, since information duties only apply when data is collected about third parties (Art. 14 GDPR), not when collected directly from the customer
options.b: The company must provide the customer with certain information already at the time of collection, including the controller's identity, the purposes and legal basis of processing, the storage period, and the customer's rights
options.c: It is enough to communicate the information only if the customer explicitly asks for it
options.d: The information duty ceases to apply once the customer signs a contract, since the contract itself counts as sufficient information

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-07.explanation: Art. 13 GDPR requires the controller to provide the data subject with certain information already at the time data is collected directly from them: among other things, the name and contact details of the controller (and, where applicable, the data protection officer), the purposes and legal basis of processing, any legitimate interests pursued, categories of recipients, the storage period or criteria for determining it, and the data subject's rights. This duty exists independently of Art. 14 GDPR, which covers data collected about third parties, and is not removed simply by signing a contract.

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-08.question: A company has an algorithm reject job applications entirely automatically, without any human reviewing or being able to intervene in the decision. Is that simply permissible?

options.a: Yes, automated decisions are always permissible as long as no accusation of discrimination becomes publicly known
options.b: Yes, because Art. 22 GDPR only applies to consumer contracts, not to recruitment processes
options.c: Generally not: under Art. 22(1) GDPR the data subject has the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing that produces legal effects; an exception only applies where necessary for a contract, authorised by law, or based on explicit consent, each requiring safeguards such as the right to obtain human intervention
options.d: No, automated decisions are prohibited under GDPR without any exception whatsoever

datenschutz-betroffenenrechte-08.explanation: Art. 22(1) GDPR generally gives the data subject the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing which produces legal effects concerning them or similarly significantly affects them - an automated rejection of a job application is a textbook example. Exceptions under Art. 22(2) GDPR only apply where necessary for a contract, authorised by law with appropriate safeguards, or based on explicit consent.

datenschutz-datensicherheit-01.question: What does Art. 32 GDPR require of controllers and processors regarding 'technical and organisational measures' (TOMs)?

options.a: A single, fixed list of measures that applies identically to every company
options.b: A level of protection appropriate to the risk, e.g. through encryption, access controls, ensuring confidentiality/integrity/availability, and regularly testing the effectiveness of the measures
options.c: Only physical measures such as lockable filing cabinets - IT security is not covered by this article
options.d: An obligation to carry out a data protection impact assessment for every processing activity

datenschutz-datensicherheit-01.explanation: Art. 32 GDPR does not prescribe a fixed checklist but a risk-appropriate level of protection: the actual scope of measures depends on the state of the art, implementation costs, and the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing as well as the risk to data subjects. It mentions, among other things, pseudonymisation/encryption, ensuring confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience, and a process for regularly testing effectiveness. A data protection impact assessment is a separate instrument under Art. 35 GDPR, not a TOM.

datenschutz-datensicherheit-02.question: A new internal applicant-tracking tool is being introduced. What does the 'privacy by design and by default' principle (Art. 25 GDPR) actually require here?

options.a: That data protection is bolted on afterwards via an update once complaints start coming in
options.b: That all available data fields are switched on by default so nothing is missing later
options.c: That only the IT department, and never business departments, is responsible for privacy settings
options.d: That data protection is built into the tool's design from the start, with the most privacy-friendly settings (e.g. minimal mandatory fields, the shortest reasonable retention periods) active by default

datenschutz-datensicherheit-02.explanation: Privacy by design means data protection requirements are built into a system's planning and development from the outset, rather than patched on afterwards. Privacy by default means that, without any active choice by the user, only the data necessary for the specific purpose is processed by default - so default settings must be privacy-friendly, not maximally data-collecting.

datenschutz-datensicherheit-03.question: Which of the following counts as a 'special category of personal data' under Art. 9(1) GDPR, requiring especially strict protection?

options.a: An employee's office number and phone extension
options.b: An employee's monthly gross salary
options.c: Information about an employee's trade union membership or state of health
options.d: An employee's home address and private mobile number

datenschutz-datensicherheit-03.explanation: Art. 9(1) GDPR lists, among others, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade union membership, genetic and biometric data, health data, and data concerning a person's sex life or sexual orientation as special categories. Salary, office numbers, or contact details are protectable personal data too, but they do not fall into this heightened-protection category.

datenschutz-datensicherheit-04.question: An employee submits a doctor's note to HR to prove sick leave. On what basis may the employer process this health data, given that it is specially protected?

options.a: Employee health data may never be processed under any circumstances, not even for sick-leave certificates
options.b: Processing is permitted because it is necessary for exercising rights and obligations arising from the employment relationship (Art. 9(2)(b) GDPR in conjunction with §26 BDSG); access should be limited to what is strictly necessary
options.c: Only with a notarised consent form from the employee - a statutory basis is not sufficient here
options.d: Only if the employee's health insurance provider grants the employer prior authorisation to process it

datenschutz-datensicherheit-04.explanation: Art. 9(2)(b) GDPR permits processing special categories of data where necessary for exercising rights and obligations under employment and social security law; §26 BDSG spells this out for German employment relationships. Sick notes are a classic, everyday example - consent is not strictly required here, but access should still be limited to a small number of authorised people (typically HR) under a need-to-know principle.

datenschutz-datensicherheit-05.question: A company plans to use new software to analyse customers' health data on a large scale, which is likely to result in a high risk to their rights and freedoms. What does Art. 35 GDPR require in such a case?

options.a: Nothing special, as long as a data processing agreement exists with the software vendor
options.b: Before processing begins, a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) must be carried out, describing among other things the planned processing operations, their necessity and proportionality, the risk to data subjects, and planned mitigation measures; if a data protection officer has been appointed, they must be consulted
options.c: A one-off verbal assessment by the IT department is sufficient, and no documentation is required
options.d: A DPIA is only required for processing carried out by public authorities, never by private companies

datenschutz-datensicherheit-05.explanation: Under Art. 35(1) GDPR, the controller must carry out a data protection impact assessment before processing where a type of processing - in particular using new technologies.

datenschutz-datensicherheit-06.question: A company regularly employs 25 people who are continuously involved in the automated processing of personal data, but has no other high-risk core business. Must a data protection officer be appointed?

options.a: Yes - under §38(1) BDSG, Germany imposes (in addition to the risk-based requirements of Art. 37 GDPR) a duty to appoint one once at least 20 people are regularly engaged in the automated processing of personal data
options.b: No, in Germany the duty to appoint one only arises once there are 250 employees, regardless of their activity
options.c: No, §38 BDSG has been completely superseded by GDPR and no longer applies
options.d: Yes, but only if the company operates in the healthcare sector

datenschutz-datensicherheit-06.explanation: Art. 37 GDPR ties the duty to appoint a data protection officer to certain risk-based criteria (e.g. core activities involving extensive monitoring or special categories of data). Independently of this, the German legislature set an additional, stricter threshold in §38(1) BDSG: non-public bodies must appoint a data protection officer once they regularly employ at least 20 people continuously engaged in the automated processing of personal data - regardless of the company's total headcount.

datenschutz-datensicherheit-07.question: A company with 50 employees regularly processes customers' health data as part of a corporate wellness programme and believes it is exempt from the duty to maintain records of processing activities (Art. 30 GDPR) because it has fewer than 250 employees. Is that correct?

options.a: Yes, the exemption under Art. 30(5) GDPR applies without exception to all companies with fewer than 250 employees
options.b: No, a record is only required for processors, never for controllers
options.c: No, the exemption for companies with fewer than 250 employees does not apply where the processing poses a risk to data subjects' rights, is not merely occasional, or involves special categories of personal data under Art. 9 GDPR - which is the case here with health data
options.d: Yes, because corporate wellness programmes are generally exempt from the scope of GDPR

datenschutz-datensicherheit-07.explanation: Art. 30(5) GDPR generally exempts companies with fewer than 250 employees from the duty to maintain a record of processing activities. However, this exemption does not apply where the processing poses a risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects, is not occasional, or includes special categories of data under Art. 9 GDPR or data relating to criminal convictions under Art. 10 GDPR. Regularly processing health data as part of a corporate programme meets this carve-out, so a record must still be maintained despite the low headcount.

datenschutz-datensicherheit-08.question: A company replaces customer names in an analytics database with random reference numbers; the mapping table between reference number and name is kept separately and specially secured. How should this procedure be classified under Art. 4(5) GDPR?

options.a: As anonymisation - the data is then no longer considered personal data and GDPR no longer applies to it
options.b: As pseudonymisation - the data can no longer be attributed to a specific person without the separately kept additional information, but it remains personal data within the meaning of GDPR
options.c: As erasure within the meaning of Art. 17 GDPR, since the real names were removed from the analytics database
options.d: As unlawful processing, since using reference numbers instead of real names is prohibited in principle

datenschutz-datensicherheit-08.explanation: Art. 4(5) GDPR defines pseudonymisation as the processing of personal data in such a way that it can no longer be attributed to a specific data subject without the use of additional information, provided that such additional information is kept separately and subject to appropriate technical and organisational measures. Unlike genuine anonymisation, re-identification via the mapping table remains possible - so the data remains personal data and continues to be subject to GDPR, even though pseudonymisation acts as a risk-reducing TOM under Art. 32 GDPR.

datenschutz-meldepflichten-01.question: On Monday morning, IT discovers that on Friday evening a database of customer data was briefly accessible unencrypted on the internet, and a risk to data subjects' rights is likely. By when must the incident generally be reported to the competent supervisory authority?

options.a: Only at the end of the current quarter, as part of the regular data protection report
options.b: Without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of the company becoming aware of it (not from the moment the incident itself occurred); if the deadline is missed, a justification for the delay must be provided
options.c: Within 72 hours of the actual moment the breach occurred, regardless of when it was discovered
options.d: There is no notification duty unless credit card data is involved

datenschutz-meldepflichten-01.explanation: The 72-hour deadline under Art. 33(1) GDPR starts running once the controller becomes aware of the breach.

datenschutz-meldepflichten-02.question: An employee briefly loses a fully encrypted company laptop that can immediately be remote-locked and wiped; no one accessed the data in the meantime. Must this incident be reported to the supervisory authority?

options.a: Not necessarily - if the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects (e.g. because of effective encryption and remote wipe), the notification duty under Art. 33(1) GDPR does not apply, though the incident should still be documented internally
options.b: Yes, every data breach without exception must be reported to the supervisory authority
options.c: No, a notification duty only exists for cyberattacks by third parties, never for lost devices
options.d: Yes, but only if the laptop was missing for more than 72 hours

datenschutz-meldepflichten-02.explanation: Art. 33(1) GDPR provides an exception to the notification duty to the supervisory authority where the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. Effective encryption and immediate remote wiping can substantially reduce such a risk. Importantly, even breaches that don't need to be reported must still be documented internally under Art. 33(5) GDPR, so the supervisory authority can review compliance if needed.

datenschutz-meldepflichten-03.question: In a cyberattack, unencrypted health data and social security numbers of several thousand customers are stolen, likely posing a high risk to those affected. Is it enough to report this incident only to the supervisory authority?

options.a: Yes, notifying the supervisory authority under Art. 33 GDPR automatically also covers informing the data subjects
options.b: No, affected individuals only need to be informed if they proactively ask the company about it
options.c: No, where a high risk is likely, the affected individuals must additionally be notified without undue delay under Art. 34 GDPR, unless one of the exceptions in Art. 34(3) GDPR applies (e.g. the affected data was effectively encrypted)
options.d: No, but notifying affected individuals is only required after a regulatory fine proceeding has concluded

datenschutz-meldepflichten-03.explanation: Art. 33 GDPR (notifying the supervisory authority) and Art. 34 GDPR (notifying data subjects) are two separate duties with different thresholds: Art. 33 already applies at any risk level, while Art. 34 only kicks in where a high risk is likely - and then it applies in addition to, not instead of, the authority notification. Exceptions under Art. 34(3) GDPR apply where the data was effectively encrypted, where subsequent measures have eliminated the high risk, or where individual notification would involve disproportionate effort (then public communication can substitute). Unencrypted stolen health data is a textbook high-risk case.

datenschutz-meldepflichten-04.question: After reviewing a minor incident, the company decides there is no duty to notify the supervisory authority because no risk to data subjects is apparent. Is the matter then closed?

options.a: Yes, without a notification duty, all further obligations regarding this incident disappear entirely
options.b: No, under Art. 33(5) GDPR, every personal data breach - including the facts, its effects, and the remedial action taken - must still be documented internally so the supervisory authority can verify compliance
options.c: No, all of the company's customers must nevertheless be informed as a precaution
options.d: Yes, documentation is only required for incidents that are subject to the notification duty

datenschutz-meldepflichten-04.explanation: Art. 33(5) GDPR requires controllers to document every personal data breach, regardless of whether notification to the supervisory authority is required. This documentation serves as evidence of accountability and allows the supervisory authority to review the company's risk assessment after the fact. Blanket notification of all customers is not required where no risk exists and would only cause unnecessary alarm.

datenschutz-meldepflichten-05.question: An external IT service provider, acting as a processor handling customer data on behalf of a company, discovers a personal data breach in its system. What must it do under Art. 33(2) GDPR?

options.a: It must report the breach directly and exclusively to the competent supervisory authority, without informing the company
options.b: It must notify the controller (the company) without undue delay after becoming aware of the breach - notifying the supervisory authority remains the controller's task
options.c: It must wait to see whether the company notices the breach itself, since processors have no notification duty of their own
options.d: It may make the notification at its own discretion within up to 30 days, since the 72-hour rule does not apply to processors

datenschutz-meldepflichten-05.explanation: Art. 33(2) GDPR requires the processor to notify the controller of a personal data breach without undue delay after becoming aware of it. Notification to the supervisory authority under Art. 33(1) GDPR, by contrast, is generally the controller's responsibility, and the controller's own 72-hour clock only starts running once it becomes aware.

datenschutz-meldepflichten-06.question: What minimum information must a notification to the supervisory authority under Art. 33(3) GDPR generally contain?

options.a: A description of the nature of the breach (where possible including categories and approximate number of data subjects), the name and contact details of a point of contact (e.g. the data protection officer), a description of the likely consequences, and the measures taken or proposed to address the breach
options.b: Only the names of all identifiable data subjects affected - any notification without a complete name list is invalid
options.c: Just a general confirmation that an incident occurred, with no further detail, since details only need to be supplied if the authority asks
options.d: A legally binding guarantee that the incident will not recur

datenschutz-meldepflichten-06.explanation: Art. 33(3) GDPR sets out the minimum content a notification to the supervisory authority must include: a description of the nature of the personal data breach (where possible, including the categories and approximate number of data subjects and records concerned), the name and contact details of the data protection officer or another point of contact, a description of the likely consequences of the breach, and a description of the measures taken or proposed to address it and mitigate its possible adverse effects. A complete list of names is not mandatory, particularly where only approximate figures are possible.

datenschutz-meldepflichten-07.question: In what form and with what minimum content must the notification of data subjects about a personal data breach under Art. 34 GDPR take place?

options.a: As a legally worded, as complex as possible letter, so as to preserve legal precision
options.b: Without any particular form or content requirements - a brief mention in the next set of contract documents is sufficient
options.c: In clear and plain language, describing the nature of the breach; the communication must also include at least the information referred to in Art. 33(3)(b), (c) and (d) GDPR, i.e. the point of contact, the likely consequences, and the remedial measures taken
options.d: Only via a public press release - individual notification is never envisaged under Art. 34 GDPR

datenschutz-meldepflichten-07.explanation: Art. 34(2) GDPR requires that the communication to the data subject describes, in clear and plain language, the nature of the personal data breach and includes at least the information and recommendations referred to in points (b), (c) and (d) of Art. 33(3) GDPR: the contact point's details, the likely consequences of the breach, and the measures taken or proposed to address it. The goal is understandable, directly actionable communication - not legal jargon and not a mere passing mention. Public communication instead of individual notification is only permitted under the narrow conditions of Art. 34(3)(c) GDPR (disproportionate effort).

datenschutz-meldepflichten-08.question: An employee, without authorisation, sells extensive customer data records to a third party on a commercial basis. What legal consequence can this employee face under the BDSG, independent of employment-law consequences?

options.a: None beyond employment law, since the BDSG only provides for fines against companies, never criminal sanctions against individuals
options.b: A criminal sanction under §42 BDSG: whoever knowingly and without authorisation transmits, on a commercial basis, non-publicly accessible personal data of a large number of people to third parties can be punished with imprisonment of up to three years or a fine; prosecution generally requires a criminal complaint
options.c: Automatic confiscation of the employee's salary in favour of the affected customers without any court proceeding
options.d: Life imprisonment, since this constitutes especially serious economic crime

datenschutz-meldepflichten-08.explanation: Section 42(1) BDSG criminalises knowingly transmitting, or otherwise making accessible, non-publicly accessible personal data of a large number of people to third parties without authorisation, where this is done on a commercial basis - imprisonment of up to three years or a fine is possible. Section 42(2) BDSG also covers unauthorised processing or fraudulently obtaining such data for payment or with intent to enrich oneself or harm another, punishable with imprisonment of up to two years. Under §42(3) BDSG, prosecution generally requires a criminal complaint. This shows that data protection violations can lead not only to fines against the company but also to individual criminal liability.

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-01.question: The company wants to outsource payroll processing to an external service provider, who needs access to employee data for this. What is mandatory before the provider may begin processing?

options.a: An informal verbal agreement is enough, as long as both sides trust each other
options.b: A written (electronic form is acceptable) data processing agreement under Art. 28 GDPR, covering, among other things, the subject matter, duration, nature and purpose of processing, categories of data, and the processor's obligations
options.c: Notarisation of the arrangement, because employee data is involved
options.d: Nothing, as long as the service provider is also based in Germany

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-01.explanation: Art. 28(9) GDPR mandates a written contract for data processing on behalf of a controller (electronic form is sufficient). Under Art. 28(3) GDPR, the contract must set out, among other things, the subject matter, duration, nature and purpose of processing, the type of personal data and categories of data subjects, and the obligations and rights of the controller. A purely verbal trust-based arrangement is not enough, regardless of where the service provider is located.

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-02.question: An engaged IT service provider wants to bring in a further subcontractor (sub-processor) for data storage. May it simply do so?

options.a: No, under Art. 28(2) GDPR a processor may not engage another processor without the controller's prior specific or general written authorisation
options.b: Yes, once a contract with the main service provider exists, any number of further subcontractors can be brought in without additional authorisation
options.c: Yes, as long as the subcontractor is based within the EU, no separate authorisation is needed
options.d: No, sub-processors are generally prohibited under GDPR

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-02.explanation: Art. 28(2) GDPR requires that a processor does not engage another processor without the controller's prior specific or general written authorisation. Where a general authorisation is given, the processor must inform the controller of intended changes so the controller can object. Being based within the EU doesn't remove this authorisation requirement, and sub-processors are not banned outright - they are simply subject to conditions.

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-03.question: A company wants to transfer customer data to a cloud provider based outside the EU/EEA. What applies here, at a conceptual level, under Art. 44 et seq. GDPR?

options.a: Such a transfer is fundamentally prohibited and never permitted
options.b: It is always enough that the customer gave prior consent by email, regardless of the destination country
options.c: The transfer needs a suitable basis, e.g. an adequacy decision by the European Commission for the destination country (Art. 45 GDPR) or appropriate safeguards such as EU Standard Contractual Clauses (Art. 46 GDPR); without such a basis, the transfer is generally not permitted
options.d: Such transfers are governed solely by the destination country's national law, not by GDPR

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-03.explanation: Transfers of personal data to third countries are only permitted under Art. 44 GDPR if a suitable basis exists: either an adequacy decision by the European Commission confirming an adequate level of protection in the destination country (Art. 45 GDPR), or appropriate safeguards such as EU Standard Contractual Clauses, binding corporate rules, or, in narrow cases, one of the derogations listed in Art. 49 GDPR. A simple email consent generally isn't sufficient as the sole, ongoing basis for regular transfers, and GDPR applies in addition to the destination country's national law, not instead of it.

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-04.question: As part of onboarding, a new employee is given access to a system containing customer data, even though their role only requires part of that data. Which principle is being violated here, and what is the correct approach?

options.a: No principle is violated, since every employee should generally have access to all company data
options.b: This is a violation of the right to data portability, since the employee could theoretically export the data
options.c: It is unproblematic as long as the employee has been bound to confidentiality under §53 BDSG, regardless of the scope of their access rights
options.d: This violates the need-to-know principle; access rights should be restricted, under the data minimisation principle, to what is actually required for the employee's task, in addition to the general duty of confidentiality under §53 BDSG

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-04.explanation: Beyond the general duty of employees to maintain confidentiality under §53 BDSG, the data minimisation principle (Art. 5(1)(c) GDPR) requires that access rights be granted on a need-to-know basis: employees should only be able to access the data actually required for their specific task. A confidentiality obligation does not substitute for technical access restrictions - both are required, not one or the other.

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-05.question: A company selects the cheapest provider for cloud storage of customer data, without checking its security measures or data protection practices. Is that compatible with Art. 28 GDPR?

options.a: No, under Art. 28(1) GDPR a controller may only work with processors that provide sufficient guarantees of implementing appropriate technical and organisational measures and ensuring processing complies with GDPR - careful selection and vetting is required
options.b: Yes, selecting a processor is not subject to any due diligence obligation as long as a contract is signed
options.c: Yes, because security measures are solely the processor's concern and create no obligation for the controller
options.d: No, but only because cheap providers are inherently considered disreputable

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-05.explanation: Art. 28(1) GDPR requires the controller to work only with processors that provide sufficient guarantees of implementing appropriate technical and organisational measures such that processing meets GDPR's requirements and safeguards data subjects' rights. This implies a certain level of due diligence in the selection process (e.g. checking certifications, references, or TOM documentation) - simply signing a contract without any vetting is not enough, regardless of how cheap the offer is.

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-06.question: The data processing agreement with an IT service provider includes an on-site audit clause. However, the provider denies the controller access and also fails to provide evidence of compliance with its obligations. Is that permissible?

options.a: Yes, a processor can refuse audits at its own discretion at any time
options.b: Yes, as long as the provider issues a written statement of no objection in return
options.c: No, but only because this involves customer data rather than employee data
options.d: No, under Art. 28(3)(h) GDPR the processor must make available to the controller all information necessary to demonstrate compliance with its obligations and allow for and contribute to audits, including inspections, conducted by the controller or an auditor mandated by the controller

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-06.explanation: Art. 28(3)(h) GDPR obliges the processor to make available to the controller all information necessary to demonstrate compliance with the obligations laid down in Art. 28 GDPR, and to allow for and contribute to audits, including inspections, conducted by the controller or an auditor mandated by the controller. A blanket refusal of audits, or a mere statement of no objection as a substitute, does not satisfy this duty - regardless of whether customer or employee data is involved.

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-07.question: A company without an adequacy decision and without EU Standard Contractual Clauses wants to transfer a customer's data on a one-off basis to a partner in a third country, relying on the customer's explicit consent given after being informed of the risks. Is that possible?

options.a: No, without an adequacy decision or Standard Contractual Clauses, any third-country transfer is prohibited without exception
options.b: Yes, Art. 49(1)(a) GDPR exceptionally permits such a transfer on the basis of explicit, informed consent - but this derogation must be interpreted narrowly and is intended for occasional, non-repetitive transfers, not as a permanent basis for systematic data flows
options.c: Yes, and this exception can also be used without limitation as a permanent basis for regular, large-scale transfers
options.d: No, consent is never a permissible basis for third-country transfers

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-07.explanation: Art. 49(1)(a) GDPR exceptionally permits a transfer to a third country where the data subject has explicitly consented after being informed of the possible risks of such a transfer. However, the derogations in Art. 49 GDPR are designed as narrowly construed exceptions to the rule, primarily intended for occasional, non-repetitive transfers - for regular, systematic, or large-scale data flows, an adequacy decision (Art. 45 GDPR) or appropriate safeguards such as Standard Contractual Clauses (Art. 46 GDPR) should instead form the actual basis.

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-08.question: An online retailer based in the USA, with no establishment in the EU whatsoever, specifically targets customers in Germany and continuously processes their order data. What does Art. 27 GDPR generally require of this company?

options.a: Nothing, since Art. 27 GDPR only applies to public authorities, not to private online retailers
options.b: Relocating the entire company headquarters to the EU
options.c: Designating, in writing, a representative in the Union who serves as a point of contact for supervisory authorities and data subjects on matters of GDPR compliance - an exception only applies for purely occasional, low-risk processing without extensive special categories of data
options.d: Merely appointing a data protection officer based in the USA

datenschutz-auftragsverarbeitung-08.explanation: Art. 27(1) GDPR generally requires controllers and processors without an establishment in the Union, but who specifically offer goods or services to people in the EU or monitor their behaviour, to designate a representative in the Union in writing. This representative serves as a point of contact for supervisory authorities and data subjects on all matters related to processing. An exception under Art. 27(2) GDPR applies, among other things, to processing that is only occasional, does not involve large-scale processing of special categories of data, and is unlikely to result in a risk to data subjects' rights, as well as for public authorities. A data protection officer based outside the EU does not substitute for this obligation.
